children.html: Measuring the Muses: Validating the Kaufman Domains of Creativity Scale (K-DOCS)
Alexander S. McKay The Pennsylvania State University
Maciej Karwowski The Maria Grzegorzewska University
James C. Kaufman University of Connecticut

The Kaufman Domains of Creativity Scale (K-DOCS) is a self-report, domain-specific measure assessing creativity in 5 domains: Everyday, Scholarly, Performance, Science, and the Arts. J. C. Kaufman (2012) provided initial evidence for the K-DOCS' factor structure. However, the factor structure requires replication and the measure has not been validated. The current study examines the factor structure of the K-DOCS and applies the Amusement Park Theoretical hierarchical model as a framework to establish validation evidence. Adults from Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) (N = 825) and Poland (N = 500) completed the K-DOCS and a measure of the Big Five. The Polish sample also completed other creativity (e.g., CAQ, creative self-beliefs) and noncreativity (e.g., intelligence, dark triad) measures. Confirmatory factor analyses indicated the factor structure of the K-DOCS was reliable. Additionally, we demonstrate convergent and discriminant validity of the 5 K-DOCS factors based on their correlations with domain-general predictors of creativity and domain-specific predictors. We also explored the existence of latent profiles and found that the measure was not well represented with a profile structure. The current study demonstrates that the K-DOCS is a reliable and valid measure for assessing domain-specific creativity.
Keywords: creativity, creativity assessment, creative self-perceptions, creative domains, measurement

Creativity is a multifaceted construct. However, many behavioral and self-report measures approach the construct with a unitary focus. Examples include divergent thinking tests, which assess creativity in general ways (with both verbal and figural versions), convergent thinking tests, which are typically verbal, and selfreport and checklist measures, which ask people to either rate their own general creativity or tally accomplishments or activities that are then summed into one broad score. This domain-general approach reasons that people who are creative in one domain are likely to be creative in other domains (Plucker, 1998). Others (e.g., Baer, 2010; J. C. Kaufman & Baer, 2002, 2004a, 2006) argue for a domain-specific approach to creativity. That is, the traits, abilities, and resources that would enable someone to be creative in one domain would not be the same that would enable that person to be creative in another domain. The Amusement Park Theoretical (APT; Baer & Kaufman, 2005; J. C. Kaufman & Baer, 2004b,

2005) hierarchical model bridges these two views and proposes four hierarchical levels of traits for creativity. The first level acknowledges that there are some traits, abilities, and resources that would be needed for any creative expression, regardless of domain. The second level consists of general thematic areas such as writing, science, and art. The third and fourth levels reflect domains (e.g., singing in the Performance domain) and microdomains (e.g., playing the guitar or piano), respectively.

It is often impractical to examine behavioral and self-report creativity across all domains, given the large number of domains and their complexity (it may be impossible to count every possible microdomain). To overcome this limitation, J. C. Kaufman's (2012) Domains of Creativity Scale (K-DOCS) provides researchers an instrument to examine creativity situated at the second and third levels—general thematic areas and domains—of the APT model across five general thematic areas of creativity: Everyday, Scholarly, Performance, Science, and Art. It is a 50-item selfreport measure developed to fill a gap in the measurement of domain-specific creativity. Previous self-report measures, although often demonstrating solid reliability (Silvia, Wigert, Reiter-Palmon, & Kaufman, 2012), were either focused on high creative achievement (e.g., Creative Achievement Questionnaire [CAQ]; Carson, Peterson, & Higgins, 2005), the general thematic area level (e.g., Creative Domain Questionnaire [CDQ]; J. C. Kaufman, 2006; J. C. Kaufman et al., 2010), or on the completion of specific creative activities (Ivcevic & Mayer, 2009). When completing the K-DOCS, people report whether they perceive themselves to be

more or less creative compared with other people of approximately the same age and life experience. In the initial article, J. C. Kaufman (2012) found that five factors were reliable and demonstrated initial construct validity by assessing how the K-DOCS factors related to the Big Five (Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Emotional Stability, and Openness to Experience).

Although the initial scale development and the scales used in research have been fruitful, the K-DOCS' factor structure has not been replicated in an independent sample and has not been validated. J. C. Kaufman (2012) focused on the K-DOCS' relationship with the Big Five, but did not examine domain-specific traits and achievement that should relate to perceptions of one's creativity within each domain. The current study applies the APT hierarchical model for validating the K-DOCS and examines both domaingeneral traits that predict scores across the domains, and domainspecific traits and achievements that predict scores within each domain. We begin by discussing domain-general predictors and then focus on domain-specific predictors to further develop the K-DOCS' nomological network. Two samples, one from Amazon's Mechanical Turk (MTurk) and one from Poland, were used to test our predictions. We also examined the K-DOCS' factor structure using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and latent profile analysis (LPA).

Drawing from the APT hierarchical model, there are a number of initial requirements, or domain-general traits, that are necessary, but not sufficient, for engaging in creative acts and behaviors (J. C. Kaufman & Baer, 2004b). The traits include the personality traits Openness to Experience, Creative Self-Beliefs, and Intelligence. Openness to Experience has consistently been shown to be related to self-report and behavioral creativity measures (Feist, 1998, 2010; Hoff, Carlsson, & Smith, 2012; McCrae, 1987). People high in Openness to Experience are likely to seek opportunities to engage in creative activities. J. C. Kaufman (2012) found that Openness to Experience had a significant positive relationship with four of the five factors; the Science factor was unrelated to Openness to Experience. Awofala and Fatade (2015) found a similar pattern of results.

Creative self-beliefs, which include creative self-efficacy (CSE) and creative personal identity (CPI), are also important motivationrelated drivers for creativity. CSE is the belief that one has the potential to be creative (Karwowski & Lebuda, 2016; Tierney & Farmer, 2002); CPI is how important creativity is to one's selfimage (Karwowski, Lebuda, Wisniewska, & Gralewski, 2013). Ford (1996) and Tierney and Farmer (2002) argued that creative self-beliefs, like CSE, are key motivators for engaging in creative activities. If creativity is an important part of one's identity, one will be motivated to engage in creative activities to maintain a positive self-view. Thus, creative self-beliefs should predict creativity across all domains.
The APT model argues that intelligence is another important trait for creativity. A certain level of cognitive functioning is important to learn and apply the necessary skills across multiple

domains of creativity. Previous research has demonstrated a positive, linear relationship between intelligence and creative achievement in general (Jauk, Benedek, Dunst, & Neubauer, 2013), and a more complex relationship with creative abilities (Jauk et al., 2013; Karwowski & Gralewski, 2013; see also Silvia, 2015, for a review). Thus, in the current study, we believe that intelligence will predict self-perceptions of one's creativity across domains.

In sum, the APT model argues that the personality trait Openness To Experience, motivation-related traits (i.e., creative selfbeliefs), and intelligence are important for creativity across all domains. Thus, we hypothesized the following:
Hypothesis 1 (H1): Scores on all five K-DOCS factors will positively relate to (a) openness to experience, (b) creative self-beliefs (i.e., CPI and CSE), and (c) intelligence.

Although there are domain-general traits that predict creativity across domains, each domain has a number of unique traits and predictors that influence one's perceptions of their domain-specific creativity. Certain predictors might be important for multiple domains, but are not universal across all domains. We discuss predictors that relate to each K-DOCS factor.

Everyday factor. The Everyday factor includes both intrapersonal and interpersonal creative behaviors. These behaviors are similar to the Big Five Extraversion and Agreeableness traits. People with higher Everyday scores are likely to engage in cooperative and prosocial situations, and report higher Extraversion and Agreeableness scores (J. C. Kaufman, 2012). Dostál, Plháková, and Záškodná (2015) found that the Everyday domain was positively related to trait empathy. Trait Empathy and Extraversion were the strongest two predictors in a regression analysis that included gender, the other Big Five factors, and trait systemizing. Agreeableness was unrelated to the Everyday factor, but it was highly correlated with empathizing, indicating the two predictors might account for the same variance.

People who also report higher scores on the K-DOCS Everyday factor are also likely to report engaging in everyday creative activities like arts and crafts. Although the Everyday factor might relate to achievement in some domains, the other K-DOCS factors are likely to be related to creative achievement more than the Everyday factor. Thus, we hypothesized the following:

Hypothesis 2 (H2): Scores on the K-DOCS Everyday factor will be primarily positively related to the Big Five traits of (a) Extraversion and (b) Agreeableness, and to (c) engaging in everyday creative activities.

Scholarly factor. The Scholarly factor reflects engaging in deep analysis and pursuits that involve gaining knowledge. Aside from Openness to Experience, the Scholarly factor is unlikely to be related to the other Big Five traits. Such intellectual creative pursuits do not necessarily have to involve (a) direct social interactions (e.g., someone can debate with another person online), (b) being friendly to another person (agreeableness), (c) self-discipline and organization (conscientiousness), or (d) emotional stability. That is, someone can perceive him- or herself to be more creative in these domains regardless of their relative standing on these traits. The factor, however, does reflect behaviors that involving

writing. Pretz and Kaufman (2015) found that the Scholarly factor was positively related to Creativity scores on a photo caption task and SAT Critical Reading scores (see also Cotter, Pretz, & Kaufman, 2016). Thus, it is likely that the Scholarly factor will be related to engaging in creative writing activities and achievements. Thus, we hypothesized the following:
Hypothesis 3 (H3): Scores on the K-DOCS Scholarly factor will be primarily positively related to (a) creative activity in writing, and (b) achievements in writing domains.

Performance factor. The Performance factor captures the extent to which someone perceives him- or herself to be creative in such activities as music, writing, and acting. This factor also captures both public and private performance. Thus, people high in extraversion will report being more creative in this domain (J. C. Kaufman, 2012; Silvia, Kaufman, & Pretz, 2009; Tavani, Caroff, Storme, & Collange, 2014). The other three Big Five factors (Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, and Emotional Stability) are unlikely to be strongly related to this factor. Further, people who report higher scores in this domain are also likely to engage in creative activities involving music, dance, and writing. They would also report some form of achievement in performance domains like music, dance, and theater and film (Carson et al., 2005). Therefore, we hypothesized the following:

Hypothesis 4 (H4): Scores on the K-DOCS Performance factor will be positively related to (a) extraversion; engaging in creativity activities involving (b) music, (c) dance, and (d) writing; and achievement in the performance-based domains of (e) music, (f) dance, and (g) theater and film.

Science factor. The Science factor focuses on whether someone perceives him- or herself to be creative in science, engineering, and math-related creative behaviors. It is unlikely that scores on this factor will be strongly related to the Big Five factors other than Openness to Experience. However, people reporting higher scores on the K-DOCS Science factor should also report engaging in creative activities such as computer programming, web development, and (more generally) in the sciences and math. They should also report achievements in science-based domains like the CAQ's Inventions and Scientific Discovery domains (Carson et al., 2005). Thus, we hypothesized the following:

Hypothesis 5 (H5): Scores on the K-DOCS Science factor will be primarily positively related to engaging in (a) sciencerelated creativity activities and reporting achievements in the science-based domains, (b) inventions, and (c) scientific discovery.

Artistic factor. The last factor, Artistic, reflects whether one perceives him- or herself to be creative in art-related activities. We predict that scores on this factor will be unrelated or have a weak relationship with the Big Five factors other than Openness to Experience. However, higher scores on this factor will be related to engaging in everyday creative activities like arts and crafts and related to activities in the Visual Arts domain. People with higher scores on this factor will also report having some level of achievement in artistic domains like the CAQ's Visual Arts and Architectural Design (Carson et al., 2005). Thus, we hypothesized the following:

Hypothesis 6 (H6): Scores on the K-DOCS artistic factor will be positively related to (a) engaging in everyday creative activities, and (b) visual arts activities; scores will also be positively related to achievements in (c) visual arts, and (d) architectural design.

There were two primary purposes of this study with the K-DOCS: examine its factor structure and provide construct and discriminant validity. Although there is some preliminary evidence of construct validity with the Big Five (J. C. Kaufman, 2012), the nomological network remains largely underdeveloped for many of the factors. We tested our hypotheses, which were rooted in the APT hierarchical model, with two large adult samples from Amazon MTurk and Poland. Using both samples, we examined the factor structure using CFA and the K-DOCS' relationship with the Big Five. In the Polish sample, we also examined the K-DOCS' relationship with a number of other constructs, both related (e.g., the CAQ) and unrelated (e.g., intelligence, dark triad) to creativity.

Notably, we did not hypothesize the K-DOCS' relationship with the CAQ domains of Humor and Culinary Arts or with the "dark triad" (Narcissism, Machiavellianism, and Psychopathy). The CAQ domains of Humor and Culinary Arts do not clearly map onto any of the five K-DOCS factors; thus, we investigated these in an exploratory manner. Additionally, only one previous study has examined the relationship among the K-DOCS factors and the dark triad (Jonason, Richardson, & Potter, 2015). We expand on this study by using a different measure of the dark triad, and investigate the relationship among these factors and their unique relationship with the K-DOCS factors after accounting for other predictors.

Using both samples, we also explored the existence of latent profiles with the K-DOCS following previous domain-specific creativity research (Silvia et al., 2009; von Stumm, Chung, & Furnham, 2011). Previous studies have found mixed results for the existence of latent classes. Silvia et al. (2009) found three classes with the CAQ, but did not find the existence of qualitative latent classes using the CDQ (J. C. Kaufman, 2006). von Stumm et al. (2011) found three classes using Batey's (2007) Biographical Inventory of Creative Behaviors. Thus, we explored the following research question in the current study:
Research Question: Do people vary in the kind of creativity (i.e., latent profiles) rather than the amount of creativity (i.e., factors) with the K-DOCS?

Participants and procedure. Participants (N - 921) signed up for the study on Amazon MTurk and were compensated with $0.50 for their participation. There were 72 (7.8%) participants with missing data on all measures who were removed from all analyses. We also classified 24 (2.6%) participants as patterned responders. Patterned responders were defined as those who clicked the same consecutive scale point for 40 or more of the 50 K-DOCS items, which reflected a z score of 3.3 or higher (z score
for 40 = 3.69). This method is similar to the Maximum Long-String index (Maniaci & Rogge, 2014; Meade & Craig, 2012).

The final sample consisted of 825 adults (89.6% of original sample; males = 412, females = 381, and 32 failed to report their sex). Participants' ages ranged from 18 to 73 years (M_{\rm age} = 33.28, SD_{\rm age} = 11.08, Mdn_{\rm age} = 30). There were 403 Asians/Asian-Americans, 278 Caucasian/European-Americans, 44 African Americans, 32 Hispanic-American/Latino(a)s, 17 Native Americans, and 50 reported "other" or failed to report their ethnicity.
Participants completed two measures in English in the following order of the K-DOCS and then a Big Five measure. After completing both measures, participants reported their demographic information.

K-DOCS. J. C. Kaufman's (2012) domain-specific creativity measure, the K-DOCS, was used. The K-DOCS is a 50-item self-report measure assessing five domains: (a) Everyday, (b) Scholarly, (c) Performance, (d) Science, and (e) Art. The instructions ask,

Compared to people of approximately your age and life experience, how creative would you rate yourself for each of the following acts? For acts that you have not specifically done, estimate your creative potential based on your performance on similar tasks.

Items were rated on a 5-point scale (much less creative to much more creative). Sample items are "Writing a nonfiction article for a newspaper, newsletter, or magazine" (scholarly) and "Making a sculpture or piece of pottery" (artistic). Cronbach's alphas were as follows: Everyday = .81, Scholarly = .85, Performance = .92, Science = .90, and Art = .89.

International Personality Item Pool (IPIP). Goldberg's (1999; Goldberg et al., 2006) 100-item Big Five scale, the IPIP, was used. The IPIP assesses the Big Five personality factors (Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Emotional Stability, and Openness to Experience). People rated the items on a 7-point scale (strongly disagree to strongly agree). There were 20 items for each factor. Sample items are "Seldom feel blue," "Am not really interested in others," and "Am full of ideas." Cronbach's alphas were as follows: Extraversion = .88, Agreeableness = .87, Conscientiousness = .89, Emotional Stability = .91, and Openness to Experience = .86.

Participants and procedure. There were 500 Polish adults (male = 284, female = 216; M_{\rm age} = 35.17, SD_{\rm age} = 5.68, range<sub>age</sub> = 26–46) that participated in the study. Participants were from an online panel by the Millward Brown Poland (Warsaw, Poland) research company that includes over 60,000 Poles who take part in various research programs once or twice per year. This online panel is a representative nationwide sample of Internet users in Poland. After signing up for the study, participants completed the survey measures in Polish in a randomized order.

K-DOCS. J. C. Kaufman's (2012) 50-item domain-specific creativity measure was used (described above). Cronbach's alphas were as follows: Everyday = .87, Scholarly = .88, Performance = .87, Science = .87, and Art = .86.

IPIP. Goldberg's (1999; Goldberg et al., 2006) 50-item scale was used, which includes 10 items per factor. Items were rated using a 5-point scale (completely inaccurately describes me to completely accurately describes me). Cronbach's alphas were as follows: Extraversion = .87, Agreeableness = .81, Conscientiousness = .80, Emotional Stability = .86, and Openness to Experience = .77.

CPI and CSE. Karwowski's (2012, 2014; Karwowski et al., 2013) 11-item measure was used to assess CPI (five items) and CSE (six items). Items were rated using a 7-point scale (definitely not to definitely yes). Cronbach's alphas were as follows: CPI = .92, and CSE = .93.

Intelligence. Sixteen items, developed as part of the International Cognitive Ability Resource Project (Condon & Revelle, 2014), were used to measure intelligence. There were four items measuring matrix reasoning, four measuring mental rotations, four dealing with letter series, and four dealing with overall reasoning. The reliability of the overall score based on the tetrachoric correlations was acceptable (\alpha = .72).

Inventory of Creative Activities and Achievements (ICAA). To measure creative activity, we used a slightly modified version of the ICAA (Jauk, Benedek, & Neubauer, 2014). Specifically, we included 33 items for creative activities in seven domains: (a) Everyday (seven items), (b) Web Development/Programming (seven items), (c) Music (four items), (d) Science (four items), (e) Dance (two items), (f) Visual Arts (four items), and (g) Writing (five items). All items devoted to achievement were omitted because achievement was assessed using the CAQ. Participants reported whether they engaged in that activity within the last year (coded 1) or did not engage in that activity (coded 0). Scale reliabilities based on the following tetrachoric correlations: Everyday = .83, Web Development/Programming = .85, Music = .88, Science = .83, Dance = .92, Visual Arts = .80, and Writing = .71.

Creative Achievement Questionnaire (CAQ). Carson et al.'s (2005) CAQ was used to measure lifetime creative achievements in 10 domains: (a) Visual Arts, (b) Music, (c) Dance, (d) Architectural Design, (e) Creative Writing, (f) Humor, (g) Inventions, (h) Scientific Discovery, (i) Theater and Film, and (j) Culinary Arts. For each domain, people place a check mark beside the sentence that applies to them depending on their level of accomplishment. The achievements in the scale are both objective and observable by others. Carson et al. (2005) provides detailed scoring instructions for the CAQ. Like many studies that use the CAQ (Silvia et al., 2012), scores were significantly skewed for all domains (z_{\text{skewness}} = 33.18-99.87). A log transformation was used to adjust the skewness. This reduced the skewness, but did not eliminate it completely (z_{\text{skewness}} = 6.24-33.81). We report results based on the log-transformed scores.

Dark triad dirty dozen. Jonason and Webster's (2010) 12-item "dirty dozen" measure was used to assess the dark triad (Narcissism, Machiavellianism, and Psychopathy). Four items measured each trait. Participants were asked how much they agreed with each item using a 7-point scale (definitely not to definitely yes). Sample items in English include "I tend to want others to admire me" (Narcissism) and "I have used deceit or lied to get my way" (Machiavellianism). Cronbach's alphas were as follows: Narcissism = .90, Machiavellianism = .91, and Psychopathy = .83.

We conducted CFAs on both samples separately using Mplus 7.0 (Muthén & Muthén, 2010) to further examine the K-DOCS' factor structure. In each sample, we conducted the CFAs in two different ways. The first CFA method for each sample included each survey item serving as an observed indicator. Because of the complexity of this model, we also conducted CFA by parceling the items into three parcels for each factor with three to four items each. To create the parcels, we used an item-to-construct balance approach. Items that had high factor loadings were combined with items that had low factor loadings. This avoids one parcel having all of the highest loading items and another with the lowest factor loadings, which can bias the results. In the current study, we identified factor loadings for each sample from the first CFA, in which all items served as indicators. For those interested in using this approach with smaller sample sizes, an exploratory factor analysis can be conducted to obtain factor loadings to create parcels.

For each sample, we conducted three CFAs: a single-factor model, a five-factor model, and a five-factor model with a second-order creativity factor (i.e., a general creativity factor). We assessed a number of indices to determine model fit. First, we examined the model chi-square statistic to compare the fit of the three models (lower values indicate a better fit). Second, we evaluated four approximate fit indexes: (a) the comparative fit index (CFI), and (b) the Tucker-Lewis index (TLI), which are goodness of fit indices (values closer to one indicate better fit); (c) the root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), which is a badness-of-fit index (values closer to zero indicate better fit); and (d) the standardized root mean square residual (SRMR), which is the standardized difference between the observed and predicted correlations (low values indicate better fit; Kline, 2011). Although

cutoffs are often employed in CFA studies, usually those provided by Hu and Bentler (1999), such values do not apply to all possible measurement models (Kline, 2011). Thus, we loosely interpret these values based on the cutoffs provided by Hu and Bentler (1999) and Browne and Cudeck (1992), and those noted by Kline (2011), which are a CFI and TLI greater than .95, and a RMSEA and SRMR less than .10.

As Table 1 shows, the results indicated that the five-factor model without a second-order Creativity factor fit the data significantly better for both samples based on chi-square difference tests. This pattern was consistent across both the CFAs with all items serving as indicators or using parcels. For the five-factor model with all items as indicators, the CFI and TLI were low in both samples. The RMSEA and SRMR were good in both samples. For the five-factor model using parcels, all of the model fit indices were good. All of the standardized and unstandardized coefficients were significant in both models (items as indicators and parcels as indicators) for both samples. Although the CFI and TLI were lower than what would be preferred, the factor structure fits with J. C. Kaufman (2012). The CFA results indicated that the five-factor model without a second-order creativity factor was the best fit for the data.

After examining the factor structure of the K-DOCS, we assessed the construct validity of the K-DOCS based on our hypotheses. In order to test for construct validity, we examined the bivariate correlations in both samples among the K-DOCS factors and Big Five factors (see Table 2), and among other factors in the Polish sample (see Table 3). In the Polish sample, we also conducted five regression analyses with each K-DOCS factor regressed on all of the predictor variables simultaneously. We also performed relative weights analysis (RWA; Tonidandel & LeBreton, 2011) as a supplement to our regression analyses. RWA, also referred to as relative importance analysis, is a statistical method for identifying each predictor's contribution to a specific criterion. This method examines the proportion of variance each predictor accounts for in the total criterion variance by considering the predictor's unique contribution and in combination with other predictors. This is useful when predictors are correlated with one another, resulting in issues with multicollinearity. For detailed overviews of RWA and how to use RWA analyses, readers are referred to Johnson (2000) and Tonidandel and LeBreton (2011, 2015). The RWA web tool (Tonidandel & LeBreton, 2015) was used to generate the R code for performing the RWA analyses. Bootstrapping based on 10,000 samples was used to obtain confidence intervals to test the significance of each relative weight (see Tonidandel, LeBreton, & Johnson, 2009, for more information).

To interpret the relative weights, if one were to sum all of the weights for the Everyday factor, they would obtain the R-squared value (within rounding error). These values can also be used to determine the proportion of variance each predictor accounted for in the total predicted variance. For example, extraversion accounted for 3.15% (rounded to .03 in Table 4) of the variance in the K-DOCS Everyday factor. One can also determine what proportion of the predicted variance each factor explained. Thus, extraversion accounted for 6.97% of the explained variance (.0315 .45 - .07). Table 4 provides the regression and RWA results.

First we tested Hypothesis 1, which stated that all five K-DOCS factors would be positively related to (a) openness to experience, (b) creative self-beliefs (CPI and CSE), and (c) intelligence. As Table 2 shows, the bivariate correlations indicated that openness to experience was significantly positively correlated with all K-DOCS factors in both samples. The strength of this relationship varied from weak to strong. The regression analyses (see Table 4), however, demonstrated that openness to experience was a significant predictor for the Scholarly and Science factors, but it did account for a significant proportion of the variance in four of the five factors in the RWA analyses (all but Performance). For creative self-beliefs, we found that bivariate correlations ranged from moderate to strong (see Table 3). In our regression and RWA analyses, CSE was a significant predictor of the Everyday, Scholarly, and Science factors, but CPI did not significantly predict any of the K-DOCS factors. Notably, the RWA analyses indicated that both CPI and CSE account for a significant portion of the variance in four of the K-DOCS factors (again, all but Performance). For intelligence, we found that it was related to the Everyday, Scholarly, and Science domains, and unrelated to the Performance and Artistic domains. The regression and RWA analyses demonstrated the same pattern of results. Thus, H1a and H1c were not supported because there were not significant predictors for all five K-DOCS factors, and H1b was partially supported because the bivariate correlations were statistically significant across all five domains and moderate to large in strength. Notably, the CAQ's Humor factor was positively related to all of the factors. In the regression analyses and RWA, Humor predicted four K-DOCS domains and accounted for a significant proportion

We then examined domain-specific traits that predict each of the K-DOCS factors. For the Everyday factor, we predicted that it would be positively related to extraversion (H2a), agreeableness (H2b), and engaging in everyday creative activities (H2c). The bivariate correlations indicated this factor was positively related to all Big Five factors, and engaging in creative activities and achievements in all domains except for Dance. The strength of the correlations ranged from weak to strong. There was also a weak positive correlation with Machiavellianism and narcissism. In the regression analysis, Everyday scores were significantly predicted by agreeableness and engaging in everyday creative activities. The RWA analysis indicated that extraversion, agreeableness, emotional stability, engaging in everyday creative activities, and the CAQ's Culinary Arts and Narcissism predicted a significant proportion of the variance in Everyday scores. Thus, H2a was partially supported, and H2b and H2c were fully supported.

For the Scholarly factor, we predicted that it would be primarily related to Creative Activity in Writing (H3a) and Achievements in Writing (H3b) domains. The Scholarly factor was weakly related to the remaining four Big Five factors in both samples, and was weak to moderately related to activities and achievements in all domains except for Dance measured by the CAQ. There was also a weak positive correlation with Machiavellianism and narcissism. For the regression analysis, the Scholarly factor was significantly predicted by engaging in everyday creative activities, science-related creative activities, writing activities, and the CAQ's Creative Writing domain. The RWA analysis indicated that multiple factors account for a significant proportion of the variance in K-DOCS Scholarly scores (see Table 4). Based on the results, H3a and H3b were supported.

We predicted the Performance factor would be positively related to extraversion (H4a); engaging in creativity activities in music (H4b), dance (H4c), and writing (H4d); and achievement in the performancebased domains of music (H4e), dance (H4f), and theater and film (H4g). The bivariate correlations indicated that the Performance was moderately related to extraversion in both samples and weakly correlated with agreeableness in the MTurk sample. It was weak to moderately correlated with engaging in creative activities, except for science, and with creative achievements in all domains except for Architectural Design and Scientific Discovery. It was also weakly positively correlated with Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and narcissism. In the regression analysis, it was positively related to extraversion, engaging in creative writing activities, achievements in music and creative writing, and marginally related to achievements in theater and film. The RWA analysis indicated that extraversion, engaging in music and writing activities, and achievements in music, creative writing, and theater and film predicted a significant proportion of the variance in Performance scores. Thus, H4a, H4d, and H4e were fully supported, and H4b, H4c, H4f, and H4g were partially supported.

For the Science factor, we predicted scores would be primarily positively related to engaging in science-related creativity activities (H5a) and reporting achievements in the science-based domains of Inventions (H5b) and Scientific Discovery (H5c). The bivariate correlations indicated that science had a weak relationship with the four remaining Big Five factors, and a weak to moderate correlation with creative activities and achievements, with the exception of everyday creative activities, dance, writing, theater and film, and culinary arts. It was also weakly positively correlated with Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and narcissism. In the regression analysis, the Science factor was significantly negatively predicted by extraversion (a suppressor effect), and positively predicted by emotional stability, engaging in web development/programming activities, and achievements in

In sum, the current study demonstrates both convergent and discriminant validity for the K-DOCS, with predicted activities and achievements being primarily related to their primary domain and unrelated to activities and achievements in other domains. It also appears to be a hybrid measure in which scores represent both aspects of the creative self as well as engagement in actual creative performance and demonstrating achievement within relevant domains. That is, people's scores are not based entirely by perceptions that they are more creative than other people without having some experience within that domain.

We next addressed our exploratory research question, which was to determine whether people vary in the kind of creativity (i.e., latent profiles) rather than the amount of creativity (i.e., factors) on the K-DOCS. We conducted LPA on both samples separately

using Mplus 7.0 (Muthén & Muthén, 2010). To determine the best-fitting model, we examined the model fit indices, considered theory, and sought to retain the most parsimonious model that replicated across the two samples. Nylund, Asparouhov, and Muthén (2007) demonstrated that the bootstrapped likelihood ratio test (LRT) and Bayesian information criterion (BIC) are good indicators of which model to choose when comparing models. Thus, we examined model fit focusing on the bootstrapped LRT analysis (based on 100 bootstrap samples) and the BIC. For the bootstrapped LRT analysis, we used 50 random starting values for the initial stage and 20 optimizations for the final stage, based on recommendations by Geiser (2012).

Regarding theory, we considered previous research examining latent profiles in creativity research (Silvia et al., 2009; von Stumm et al., 2011), which indicated we would find between two and five profiles. To be thorough, we examined up to a seven-profile model. However, solutions with fewer profiles were preferred. We sought to avoid small profiles (i.e., less than 5% of the sample) because they can be difficult to replicate. By using two samples differing on demographic characteristics (i.e., nationality), we increased the generalizability of our final model and interpretation (Geiser, 2012).

As Table 5 shows, the bootstrapped LRT and BIC indicated that the seven-profile solution was the best-fitting model for both samples. However, warnings in the output for both samples indicated that the seven-profile model was to be avoided. Additionally, there were a number of small profiles (<5% of the sample) in these models. We examined the six-profile model and found that the pattern of results was different across the two samples and that the number of people within each profile differed. In the Polish sample, the five-profile and six-profile models differed in terms of the qualitative profiles that emerged. Thus, the six-profile solution was not ideal. We then focused on the five-profile and four-profile models. The five-profile model fit the data well, but did not replicate across the two samples (see Figure 1), causing us to reject this solution. We therefore examined the four-profile model and

The four-profile solution in both samples indicated the profiles differed quantitatively rather than qualitatively (see Figure 1). The four classes were (a) a low profile, (b) a moderately low profile, (c) a moderately high profile, and (d) a high profile. The proportion of the sample in the low profile for the Polish sample was low (less than 5%). However, this class was consistent in both samples, which is why we retained this solution. Table 6 shows the average class assignment probabilities. For people in the MTurk samples, for whom Class 1 was the most likely class, the chance of belonging to Class 1 was 90%, and the chance of belonging to Class 2 was 10%; the chance of people belonging to either Class 3 or Class 4 was zero. The results from the LPA, together with the CFA results, indicated that the K-DOCS is better represented by a factor structure than it is with a profile structure. Although there was some evidence of qualitative profiles in the five-profile models, these profiles were unstable across samples and are difficult to interpret.

The K-DOCS is a relatively new measure for assessing domain-specific creativity in five domains: Everyday, Scholarly, Performance, Science, and Art. Research utilizing the K-DOCS has demonstrated partial evidence of construct validity. However, the measure's factor structure required further testing and construct validity remained to be assessed. The purpose of the present study was to examine its facture structure and to determine whether the K-DOCS is a valid measure. We applied the APT hierarchical model and examined both domain-general traits and general thematic predictors for each K-DOCS factor, and tested six hypotheses and one research question.

We found that the K-DOCS was best represented by a five-factor model without a second-order Creativity factor. This finding was consistent in both samples, but it did not align with previous research using self-report creativity measures. J. C. Kaufman, Cole, and Baer (2009) found that the 56-item, seven-factor CDQ was best represented as a seven-factor model with a second-order factor. Although there is some overlap between the K-DOCS and CDQ, the two measures have different subscales and assess different perceptions of one's creativity. The CDQ assesses one's self-rated creativity across broad areas, whereas the K-DOCS assesses how one perceives their creativity on specific activities compared with other people. The CDQ might ask, "How creative are you at algebra/trigonometry?" In contrast, the K-DOCS would ask, "Compared to people of approximately your age and life experience, how creative are you at solving an algebraic or geo-

For the first hypothesis, we predicted that the domain-general traits would predict all five K-DOCS factors. We took an "all-ornothing" approach for this hypothesis and failed to find support. We found that openness to experience, CPI, and CSE were related to four of the domains (all except Performance). Intelligence was related to three of the domains; it was unrelated to Performance and Artistic. Some support for the hypothesis was found in the pattern of correlations, regression results, and RWA analyses, which indicated that engaging in and having achievements in a domain was related to perceiving one's self to be more creative than others in that domain. Although some level of openness to experience, motivation, and intelligence is important for general

creativity, the domains of Performance and Artistic might rely on other skills and abilities. For example, Performance might require kinesthetic abilities for dance and knowledge about musical notes. The Artistic domain may depend on having high aesthetic values and visual-spatial abilities. Thus, other skills or traits may be dominant for these domains, which might indicate why engaging in and having achievements in these domains were the strongest predictors for K-DOCS ratings.

The only predictor that emerged as a domain-general trait was achievement in humor. Humor was moderately related to the five K-DOCS factors and accounted for a significant portion of the variance in all five domains. Although the weak relationships preclude us from overinterpreting this finding, it is worth noting past studies have shown that layperson conceptions of creativity

often include humor (Sternberg, 1985), and that having a broad sense of humor (i.e., finding many different types of things funny) is associated with higher creativity (Chang, Chen, Hsu, Chan, & Chang, 2015). Further, humor tends to be associated with a wide spectrum of positive attributes (Earleywine, 2010).

For the remaining hypotheses (Hypotheses 2– 6), the results generally supported our predictions. Engaging in domain-specific activities and having achievements in the respective domains had the strongest bivariate correlations and were the strongest predictors based on the regression and RWA results. For example, the Science domain was more strongly related to participating and achievement in creative science-related activities as opposed to doing so in art or dance. Additionally, the CAQ's Culinary Arts domains accounted for a significant proportion of the variance in the Everyday factor and none of the other factors. These results suggest both convergent and discriminate validity for the K-DOCS.
Beyond validating the K-DOCS, we also examined its relationship with the dark triad. Jonason et al. (2015) found that

narcissism was positively related to all five factors; psychopathy was positively related to Performance and Science; and Machiavellianism was positively related to Scholarly and Performance. The bivariate correlations in our study were fairly consistent with their findings using a different measure of the dark triad, but were smaller in strength. In our regression and RWA analyses, these traits did not emerge as explaining unique variance in the five K-DOCS factors with the exception of narcissism, which predicted a significant proportion of variance in the Everyday factor.

In the current study, we also explored whether the K-DOCS could be sufficiently represented by a profile structure (Research Question). We found four profiles in both samples that differed quantitatively rather than qualitatively. Although qualitative profiles emerged in the five-profile solution, this solution was inconsistent across the two samples. Thus, the K-DOCS is better represented by a factor structure.
Overall, the results align with the APT hierarchical model (Baer & Kaufman, 2005; J. C. Kaufman & Baer, 2004b). The domain-

general traits were related to the majority of the five K-DOCS factors; further, engaging in and having achievements in related domains differentially predicted the five factors. By applying the APT framework in the current study, we were able to develop and test key hypotheses that lend support to the K-DOCS as a theoretically and psychometrically valid measure of self-perceptions of creativity.

Although the study provides evidence of the K-DOCS being a reliable and valid measure, we acknowledge a number of limitations and possible areas for future research. First, we did not accurately capture the necessity of the domain-general traits for creativity with our analyses. Rather we examined their sufficiency. Identifying traits that are necessary, but not sufficient, cannot accurately be captured using correlational or regression analyses (Dul, 2016). For example, a high SAT score is necessary for acceptance into a prestigious university, but it is not sufficient. Every prestigious school receives many more applications with high SAT scores than it can possibly accept. A student who is admitted will also likely have a strong statement of purpose, a high GPA, glowing letters of recommendation, and engage in numerous and diverse extracurricular activities. The same can be said for creativity. There are some necessary conditions for any creativity to occur; J. C. Kaufman and Baer (2004b) articulate them as a basic level of intelligence, some level of motivation, and a supportive environment, whereas this study operationalized these factors as Intelligence, Creative Self-Beliefs, and Openness to Experience. Although it is reasonable to say that our findings support the necessity of these factors, we have not shown that any of them are sufficient for creativity.

How might this limitation be avoided in the future? One possibility can be found in a newer statistical technique that can examine necessity: necessary condition analysis (NCA; Dul, 2015). However, given that our measure of intelligence was short (16 items), and that we wanted to examine multiple general thematic area predictors as well, we felt it was inappropriate to utilize this technique in our study. Future research should consider using NCA to examine the necessity of intelligence and other domain-general traits.
Second, we did not examine environmental factors in the current study. The APT hierarchical model argues that environmental factors play an important role for domain-general and domain-

specific creativity. We were primarily interested in examining person-centered predictors rather than examining situational factors to validate the K-DOCS. Future research should consider expanding on the current study by also examining different environmental factors that predict creativity across the K-DOCS factors.

Third, we used the IPIP to measure the Big Five. The Openness to Experience factor from this measure has been referred to as a measure of intellect/imagination (see Mussel, 2013), which might have influenced the pattern of results in the current study. In a previous study, Mussel, McKay, Ziegler, Hewig, and Kaufman (2015) examined the relationship between the K-DOCS and the three operations of the theoretical intellect framework (think, learn, and create). In a series of latent regression analyses, controlling for general intellect scores, they found that the three intellect operations differentially predicted the K-DOCS factors. The Performance and Artistic factors were positively predicted by the create operation, whereas the Everyday, Scholarly, and Science factors were more strongly positively predicted by either the think or learn operations. Thus, future research should consider the subdimension of Openness to Experience when using the K-DOCS and when assessing domain-specific creativity. Future research could utilize the openness/intellect distinction (DeYoung, 2015; DeYoung, Quilty, & Peterson, 2007; S. B. Kaufman, 2013; S. B. Kaufman et al., 2016), the theoretical intellect framework (Mussel, 2013; Mussel et al., 2015), or other measures assessing subfacets of Openness to Experience (e.g., Woo et al., 2014).

Fourth, we measured general intelligence rather than specific intelligence factors. Although many studies of creativity and intelligence use this approach (J. C. Kaufman, 2009), more recent conceptions of intelligence tend to be multifaceted. For example, the Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) theory splits Intelligence into many different factors, such as Crystallized (acquired knowledge), Fluid (novel problem-solving), Visual Processing, Short-Term Memory, and Long-Term Memory (McGrew, 2009). Our Intelligence measure was primary comprised of fluid and visual processing items, yet the CHC Long-Term Memory factor is more associated with creativity (Avitia & Kaufman, 2014; J. C. Kaufman, 2015). So the actual relationship between the K-DOCS and intelligence might be quite different if a more nuanced measure of IQ was utilized.

Last, future research could also examine domains and microdomains within each of the K-DOCS' broader areas. For example, research could focus on predictors of musical creativity and theater and film creativity separately. This type of analysis has already begun. Tavani et al. (2014) utilized seven items from the K-DOCS' Performance domain that assess perceptions of one's creativity in music.

One roadblock to using this approach is that most established measures of creativity take a domain-general approach. It is possible to examine many different domains (or microdomains) by analyzing specific products using the consensual assessment technique (Amabile, 1996). The complication is that this technique requires expert (or quasi-expert) raters, which can be both time-consuming and expensive to obtain (J. C. Kaufman & Baer, 2012; J. C. Kaufman, Baer, Cropley, Reiter-Palmon, & Sinnett, 2013).

The goal of the present study was to validate and further develop the nomological network of the K-DOCS. Each domain was differentially related to constructs associated with various domaingeneral traits and with domain-specific achievements and engagement. We also found that the K-DOCS was better represented with a factor structure rather than with a profile structure. Overall, the results demonstrate that the K-DOCS is a reliable and valid measure for assessing self-perceptions of domain-specific creativity.

Members of Underrepresented Groups: Reviewers for Journal Manuscripts Wanted

If you are interested in reviewing manuscripts for APA journals, the APA Publications and Communications Board would like to invite your participation. Manuscript reviewers are vital to the publications process. As a reviewer, you would gain valuable experience in publishing. The P&C Board is particularly interested in encouraging members of underrepresented groups to participate more in this process.
If you are interested in reviewing manuscripts, please write APA Journals at Reviewers@apa.org. Please note the following important points:
• To be selected as a reviewer, you must have published articles in peer-reviewed journals. The experience of publishing provides a reviewer with the basis for preparing a thorough, objective review.

• To be selected, it is critical to be a regular reader of the five to six empirical journals that are most central to the area or journal for which you would like to review. Current knowledge of recently published research provides a reviewer with the knowledge base to evaluate a new submission within the context of existing research.

• To select the appropriate reviewers for each manuscript, the editor needs detailed information. Please include with your letter your vita. In the letter, please identify which APA journal(s) you are interested in, and describe your area of expertise. Be as specific as possible. For example, "social psychology" is not sufficient—you would need to specify "social cognition" or "attitude change" as well.
• Reviewing a manuscript takes time (1– 4 hours per manuscript reviewed). If you are selected to review a manuscript, be prepared to invest the necessary time to evaluate the manuscript thoroughly.

APA now has an online video course that provides guidance in reviewing manuscripts. To learn more about the course and to access the video, visit http://www.apa.org/pubs/authors/reviewmanuscript-ce-video.aspx.
